notes.description:
Five weeks to Mammoth Tuff, Saturday 19 September — plus this easy lead-in weekend.

———

YOUR FULL GUIDE
{guide_url}

Fourteen sections covering zones, fuelling, recovery, kit, race week, race day, gravel skills and altitude. There is a PDF on that page if you would rather keep a copy or print it.

Read sections 1 and 2 before Monday. The rest keeps.

———

ONE SETTING TO FIX
Your TrainingPeaks account holds an FTP of 240. The plan is built off the 250 you gave me. Wednesday's test settles the argument — until then, treat the watts TP shows you as approximate, and after the test put the new number in: Settings > Zones > Power. Two minutes.

———

HOW THE WEEK WORKS
Monday is off, every week, as you asked. Tuesday and Thursday carry the quality plus thirty minutes of strength. Saturday is the long ride and everything protects it. Wednesday and Friday are steady aerobic riding, Sunday is endurance.

If a week falls apart, protect Saturday and one quality day and let the rest go.

———

READING THE WORKOUTS
Every session gives you power as a percentage of FTP, plus an RPE. You ride with a power meter, so the percentages are your primary handle — they become exact watts the moment your FTP is set right. When power and RPE disagree late in a long ride, believe RPE.

Titles carry the shape: what it is, how long, how hard.

———

NEED THIS ADJUSTED?
Email me at gravelgodcoachingatgmail.com. Tell me what happened and what you want changed — a week that fell apart, a session that felt wrong, travel, illness, a day that no longer works. Adjusting a plan is normal and costs you nothing. Grinding through something that is not working costs you weeks.
notes.title: START HERE — Your Mammoth Tuff Plan

notes.description:
Two rides and a rest day before the plan proper. Nothing here is training — it is arrival. Easy spin, endurance ride, then Sunday completely off so you start Monday's week fresh.

Your last few months have been sporadic. That is fine — it is what week one is for.
notes.title: WEEKEND 0 — EASY START

notes.description:
Wednesday is the session that matters: a 20-minute all-out FTP test. Everything downstream scales off the number it produces, so give it a real go. On a trainer, use RESISTANCE or LEVEL mode, not ERG — ERG will hold you at the old number instead of letting you show what you can do.

Thursday is a 3-minute all-out effort after a long easy spin-up. It is three minutes. It will feel longer.

The rest of the week is steady endurance with your first two strength sessions (Tuesday and Thursday, thirty minutes, everything doable at home — video links inside each workout).

One rule for the whole week, given the sporadic months behind you: if a session feels harder than its description says it should, stop and tell me. That is data, not failure.
notes.title: WEEK 1 — TEST WEEK

notes.description:
The mental side of this gets the same treatment as the physical: a few short things, practised until they are automatic. This is the first.

———

CENTERING YOUR BIOLOGY
Under stress your breathing goes shallow and fast, which tells your nervous system there is a threat, which makes you feel worse, which makes the breathing worse. You can break that loop from either end, and breathing is the end you control.

———

THE 6-2-7 FORMULA
Breathe in for 6, hold for 2, out for 7. The long exhale is the active ingredient — it is what drops your heart rate.

Do it for two minutes before a hard session, and again in the first ten minutes of a race when everything feels too fast. Practise it now, on easy days, so it is available when you need it. A technique you have never rehearsed will not show up on race day.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 1 — Breathing, And Why It Is First

notes.description:
Take your average power for the 20-minute effort and multiply it by 0.95. That is your FTP.

Put it into TrainingPeaks: Settings > Zones > Power. Every workout in the plan then shows real watts instead of percentages of a number we were arguing about.

———

THEN SEND IT TO ME
Reply with the number and how the test felt — whether you paced it well, whether you had more at the end, whether you had to stop. That tells me as much as the number does, and it is the first point where I can adjust anything that is aimed wrong.

{coach_email}
notes.title: AFTER TODAY'S TEST — Send Me The Number

notes.description:
Your gut is trainable and it needs the repetitions, so the target climbs with the long rides rather than appearing on race morning.

22 Aug — 50 g/hr
29 Aug — 60
5 Sep — 65-70 (race rate, on the five-hour rehearsal)
12 Sep — 55
Race day — 66

Sessions under 90 minutes are not on the ladder — eat what you like on those.

Where an individual workout quotes a different number, use the ladder. It is built for your body weight and for how long you will actually be out there.

———

WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE
Roughly 30-35 g every 25-30 minutes, starting inside the first half hour. Set a timer. Read the labels rather than counting items — gels run anywhere from 20 to 40 g and drink mixes vary as much, so "a gel every half hour" can quietly leave you well short.

Hunger is a lagging indicator. By the time you feel empty you are already an hour behind.

———

FLUID
Drink to thirst. 500-750 ml/hr is a starting estimate to adjust for heat and sweat rate, not a quota to hit. 500-1000 mg sodium per hour.

Do not force fluid beyond thirst across a long day. The simple check is that you should finish a shade lighter than you started, never heavier.
notes.title: FUELLING — The Ladder

notes.description:
The first full build week. Tuesday is VO2 — three five-minute efforts at 110%, with a tempo flush after. Thursday is 3x10 minutes at 90%, the honest kind of uncomfortable. Friday is cadence work: high-rpm blocks at 100-120, which will feel ridiculous until it doesn't.

Saturday is the big one: Race Sim Act 1 — five hours shaped like Mammoth itself. A punchy start, a long disciplined grind with low-cadence climbing, and a structured finale on tired legs. It is also your first fuelling rehearsal: 60 g/hr, per the ladder.

Start practising your race food this Saturday. Whatever you plan to eat at Mammoth, eat it then.
notes.title: WEEK 2 — BUILD

notes.description:
———

THE CHESS GAME
Somewhere in hour four your brain will offer you: "I can't hold this." "Everyone is stronger than me." "I should have trained more."

You do not have to argue with any of it. Arguing is playing the game. The move is to notice the thought, name it as a thought rather than a fact, and go back to what you were doing — the next ten miles, the next thing to eat.

———

PERFORMANCE STATEMENTS
Have two or three short phrases ready before race day. Not affirmations — instructions. Things like: "Smooth and steady." "Eat now." "Ride your own effort."

Short, specific, actionable. Write them down this week and use them on your long rides, so by 19 September they are a habit rather than something you are trying for the first time while suffering.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 2 — You Are Not Your Thoughts

notes.description:
The biggest week of the plan. Tuesday is Norwegian-style threshold — 3x8 minutes at 106% with full recoveries. Thursday is the hardest weekday session you will do: two hours blending 30/30 surges with a long block at 90%. Respect it — nothing else that day but the thirty minutes of strength.

Saturday is the full dress rehearsal: five hours, race kit, race bike, race tyre pressure, race food at 65-70 g/hr — the actual race rate. Nothing about race day should be new to you after this ride.

Everything after Saturday points at freshness. Do not add anything this week.
notes.title: WEEK 3 — PEAK

notes.description:
You are through the hardest part of the build's first half. Worth an honest audit before the peak week:

· Are you finishing the Saturday rides, or surviving them?
· Is your sleep holding up? (You flagged it as fair — this is the week it matters.)
· Are you hungry all the time, or has your appetite gone?
· Is anything hurting that was not hurting three weeks ago?
· Are you looking forward to riding, or dreading it?

Two or more of those pointing the wrong way and we should take something out now rather than in race week.

———

NEED THIS ADJUSTED?
Email me at gravelgodcoachingatgmail.com. Adjusting a plan is normal and costs you nothing. Grinding through something that is not working costs you weeks.
notes.title: CHECK-IN — Two Weeks In. How Is It Landing?

notes.description:
Mammoth sits at 7,900-8,100 feet the whole way. It is the defining feature of the event, and it is two separate problems.

———

THE AIR
At that altitude expect roughly 5% off your FTP, breathing that is harder from the gun, and a heart rate that stops being reliable — it can sit high at easy paces and refuse to climb when you push late. Do not chase your familiar numbers up there. Ride to RPE and power.

If you can arrange a week or more at altitude before the race, that is best. If not, arriving close to the start is a reasonable compromise — the first days at altitude are usually the roughest, so either be there long enough to adapt or short enough not to pay for it.

———

THE SUN
At 8,000 feet there is a third less atmosphere filtering UV. You will burn faster than the temperature suggests, and sunburn measurably raises how hard everything feels. Sunscreen before the start and again at an aid station — do not skip it because the morning is cold.

Mid-September mornings up there start cold and warm fast. Plan a layer you can lose and actually carry: arm warmers and a gilet that pack small beat a jacket you will not want to hang on to.

The full altitude playbook is section 14 of your guide.
notes.title: ALTITUDE AND SUN — Plan For Both

notes.description:
———

BUILD IT NOW
Think of three or four times you rode genuinely well. Not podiums necessarily — the day you held a wheel you did not expect to, the climb that went better than it should have, the ride you finished when you wanted to stop.

Write them down in detail. What you could see, what your legs felt like, what you told yourself.

———

WHY
Confidence is not a mood, it is evidence. When it deserts you at mile 60 you will not be able to conjure it, but you can recall it — and specific, sensory memories are far more usable than a general belief that you are fit.

Read them the night before the race. Run one of them in your head on the start line.

———

WHO YOU ARE ON THE BIKE
One more: finish the sentence "I am the kind of rider who ______" three times. How you describe yourself shapes what you attempt. If everything you write is about surviving, that is worth noticing before race day — you have done the work to say something better.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 3 — Your Highlight Reel

notes.description:
While yesterday is still fresh, note:

· What you ate and when. Did you hit 65-70 g/hr, or drift?
· What your stomach did in hours three to five.
· What chafed, rubbed, went numb or ached.
· What you ran out of.
· How the last hour felt, honestly.
· What you would change about the pacing.

Send it to me. Two weeks is enough to fix kit, fuelling and pacing — but only if we know what broke.

{coach_email}
notes.title: REHEARSAL DEBRIEF — Write It Down And Send It

notes.description:
You will feel worse before you feel better this week. That is the taper working, and it is normal to feel flat and slightly anxious in the middle of it.

Volume drops hard but the legs stay awake: Tuesday openers, Wednesday thirty-fifteens — high stimulus, low damage — Thursday high-cadence spinning, and Saturday a hundred easy minutes with a six-second burst every quarter hour.

Finish Saturday feeling like you could have done another hour. If you finish it tired, you overcooked it.
notes.title: WEEK 4 — TAPER

notes.description:
———

WHICH COURSE YOU ARE ON
Your entry said 100 miles — Mammoth's actual courses are 41, 67 and 89. For UCI qualifying they split by age: the 89 for riders 19-49, the 67 for 50 and over. At 49, if you are qualifying, you are on the 89: roughly seven hours and 7,500 feet of climbing. Check your entry and tell me which it is.

Your training does not change between them. Your pacing and the amount of food you carry do: longer course, more conservative first half, more total fuel.

———

ALTITUDE
The race sits at 7,900-8,100 feet the whole way. At any given effort your power and speed will be lower than at home and breathing will be harder from the gun. Heart rate is the unreliable one — do not chase your familiar numbers. Ride to RPE and power.

———

PACING
Start easier than feels right. At altitude an early overspend is not repaid later — it compounds. First third RPE 4-5, middle third 5-6, and spend what is left in the last third. People will come past you in the first hour. A good number of them come back.

———

WHEN IT GETS BAD
It will, somewhere. Break what remains into ten-mile pieces and ride the piece you are in. Eat something. Often it passes inside twenty minutes.

What is not a bad patch, and means stop and find a medic: chest pain, confusion, or a headache that keeps building.

———

FRIDAY NIGHT
Bottles mixed. Food in pockets and counted against where the aid stations actually are. Kit laid out. Tyres checked. Computer charged. Then stop.

———

WORTH RE-READING THIS WEEK
Sections 11, 12 and 14 of your guide — Race Week, Race Day and Altitude: {guide_url}

———

ANY LAST QUESTIONS
Send them this week rather than Friday night — gravelgodcoachingatgmail.com. Nothing is too small to ask about.
notes.title: RACE WEEK — Mammoth Tuff, Saturday 19 September

notes.description:
Nothing you do this week adds fitness. Plenty could subtract it.

Tuesday is Stars In Your Eyes — short 20/30/40-second efforts, going hard but not reaching for the last five percent. Thursday is fifty easy minutes. Wednesday is off. Friday is travel, number pickup, bike check — and openers to prime the legs for Saturday.

Sleep is the training this week. Eat normally and a little more than feels necessary.
notes.title: WEEK 5 — RACE WEEK

notes.description:
———

MUSIC
If music helps you, build the playlist this week rather than on the drive up. Be deliberate: something calm for the morning, something that lifts you for the last hour. What you listen to before a start genuinely shifts how you feel at it — pick accordingly rather than by accident.

———

THE NIGHT BEFORE
Read your highlight reel. Run through your performance statements. Then stop thinking about the race — the work is done and rehearsing it further only costs sleep.

———

ON THE LINE
Two minutes of 6-2-7 breathing. Everyone around you will look faster and more organised than you feel. They are not.

Your first job is to start easier than feels right. Everything after that is eating on time and riding your own effort.

You have done the work. Go and use it.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 4 — The Last Three Days

notes.description:
Nothing today. Eat, drink, sleep.

If the legs feel stiff tomorrow, thirty minutes of easy spinning helps more than sitting still. Otherwise take the week easy and let it land.

When you have had a day to think about it, send me your race notes: what worked, what you would change, what surprised you, and what you want to do next. That is what the next plan gets built on.

———

WHAT'S NEXT
Five weeks of structure got you to this start line. The bigger gains are in what comes after — the base you build when there is no race breathing down your neck.

I see a Media Maratón on your calendar for 4 October. If you want a two-week bridge that gets you there with legs instead of leftovers, say the word — that is a quick build.

And if Mammoth left you wanting a bigger target: reply with the race and the date, and we will do this again with more runway. Six weeks was the trailer. A twelve-week block is the film.

{coach_email}

workouts.title: Cadence Work - 100-120rpm - 52min - RPE5-6

workouts.description:
Race simulation #1 — a five-hour day in three acts, shaped like Mammoth Tuff.

ACT 1 — THE START (first ~40min): 10min high-cadence Z3, then 5x30/30 and three 20-second attacks with 40 seconds hard on the wheel. This is what the first miles at Mammoth do to you: fast, punchy, everyone overspending.

ACT 2 — THE GRIND (middle ~2h): two long blocks of steady Z2, each ending in 20 minutes of low-cadence climbing at 50-60rpm. Red Rock Canyon is a long seated grind at altitude — this is its rehearsal. Stay in the saddle, keep the pressure even.

ACT 3 — THE FINALE (final ~45min): one pyramid (3min each at 80/90/100/90/80%) then steady Z2 on tired legs. The race is decided here by whoever still has the discipline to ride structure when everything hurts.

EXECUTION:
- Ride Acts 1 and 3 at their targets; ride Act 2 disciplined and bored. Boredom is the skill.
- Fuel at 60 g/hr per the ladder. Practise eating ON the low-cadence climbs — that is where race-day fuelling actually fails.

———

workouts.description:
Race simulation #2 — the full dress rehearsal. Race kit, race bike, race tyre pressure, race food. Nothing about race day should be new after today.

ACT 1 — THE START (first ~40min): 10min high-cadence Z3, then 5x30/30 and three 20-second attacks with 40 seconds hard on the wheel. This is what the first miles at Mammoth do to you: fast, punchy, everyone overspending.

ACT 2 — THE GRIND (middle ~2h): two long blocks of steady Z2, each ending in 20 minutes of low-cadence climbing at 50-60rpm. Red Rock Canyon is a long seated grind at altitude — this is its rehearsal. Stay in the saddle, keep the pressure even.

ACT 3 — THE FINALE (final ~45min): two pyramids (3min each at 80/90/100/90/80%, 5min between) then steady Z2 on tired legs. The race is decided here by whoever still has the discipline to ride structure when everything hurts.

EXECUTION:
- Ride Acts 1 and 3 at their targets; ride Act 2 disciplined and bored. Boredom is the skill.
- Fuel at 65-70 g/hr — the actual race rate. Then write the debrief (see Sunday's note).

———

FUELLING: On the ladder today — 65-70 (race rate) g carbs/hr, first bite inside 30 minutes, then every 25-30 minutes. Where this workout quotes a different number, the ladder wins (see the FUELLING note). This is your full race-rate rehearsal — race kit, race tyres, race food.

workouts.description:
Three sets of nine very short, very hard efforts with barely any rest. High stimulus, low damage — it keeps the top end awake through the taper without leaving a mark on your legs for Saturday.

9 x (30 seconds hard / 15 seconds easy), three times through, with 4 minutes easy between sets. RPE 9 on the efforts and high cadence — spin them, do not grind them.

These should feel sharp and almost fun. If set three is a fight, stop after two and spin. Freshness beats one more set this close to the race.

HEART RATE (you ride on feel and HR, so these are your real handles):
Recovery under 112 bpm · Endurance 114-137 bpm · Tempo 139-155 bpm · Threshold 157-173 bpm · Hard 175 bpm and above
Off your threshold HR of 165. HR lags effort by a minute or two on climbs and drifts up late in long rides at the same effort — that drift is normal. When HR and RPE disagree, trust RPE.
Note: your TrainingPeaks account still holds old threshold settings — use the bands above, not the zones TP displays, until you have updated them (see the START HERE note).

workouts.title: Openers v1.1 - 43min - RPE7

workouts.description:
Race day. You have done the work.

HOW LONG YOUR DAY IS. Your entry said 100 miles; Mammoth's courses are 41, 67 and 89. At 49 the UCI qualifying split puts you on the 89 — the TUFFEST, roughly 7 hours with 7,500 feet of climbing. This calendar entry is set to 6:50 and 292 TSS on that assumption. If you are on the 67, expect closer to five hours and ignore those numbers.

PACING. The whole race sits at 7,900-8,100 feet, and at altitude an early overspend is not repaid later — it compounds. First third at RPE 4-5, middle third 5-6, and spend what is left in the last third. The first hour will feel absurdly easy and you must let it. People will come past you early. A good number of them come back.

CLIMBS. Ride them at your effort, not the group's. Target the G-Spot zone (88-94% FTP) only on the shorter rises; on the long climbs stay conservative.

HR. At altitude heart rate stops being reliable — it can sit high at easy paces and refuse to climb when you push late. Do not chase your usual numbers. Ride to RPE and power.

FUELLING. 66 g of carbs per hour (your range: 59-73) — about 455 g over the day. First bite inside 30 minutes, then every 25-30 minutes on a timer. You rehearsed this on 5 September; nothing new today. Pre-race: 100-150 g carbs, 3-4 hours before the start.

HYDRATION. Drink to thirst — 500-750 ml/hr as a starting estimate, adjusted for heat. 500-1000 mg sodium per hour. Do not force fluid beyond thirst across a long day; finish a shade lighter than you started, never heavier.

WHEN IT GETS BAD. It will, somewhere. Break what remains into ten-mile pieces and ride the piece you are in. Eat something. Often it passes inside twenty minutes. Chest pain, confusion, or a headache that keeps building is not a bad patch — stop and find a medic.

FRIDAY NIGHT CHECKLIST.
- Bike mechanically sound, tyres at race pressure
- Bottles mixed, food in pockets and counted against the aid stations
- Electronics charged; spare tube, CO2, multi-tool
- Race number attached, drop bags ready if applicable
Then stop. Sleep is the last workout.
